chapter_title: Setting Up a DApp Development Environment

screens.title: Setting Up a DApp Development Environment
screens.subtitle: Bootstrap your frontend, add a Web3 library, and connect to a local Ethereum node for fast development.

narration.text: In this lesson you'll build a reliable DApp development environment so you can iterate quickly and safely. We'll cover how to initialize a modern JavaScript project with React or Next. js, add a Web3 library such as Ethers. js, and connect your frontend to a local blockchain like Hardhat for testing. You will also learn how to manage environment variables properly so sensitive keys and changing contract addresses don't leak into your client bundle. A good environment reduces friction: it lets you run a local node, deploy a contract, and immediately test UI interactions without spending gas or waiting on public testnets. For example, you can run a Hardhat node locally and point your Next. js app at its RPC endpoint for read-only data, or connect a browser wallet like MetaMask for signing transactions. Common pitfalls include hardcoding addresses, committing private keys, and mismatched library versions. Over the upcoming screens we’ll walk through concrete commands, sample utility code for provider selection and signing, project layout recommendations, and a hands-on activity that gets a Next. js app connected to a local Hardhat network. By the end you’ll have a repeatable setup that supports development, staging, and production workflows.

keyIdea.title: Foundation for fast, safe DApp iteration
keyIdea.text: A structured project with a Web3 library and a local node lets you develop, test, and debug without real gas costs or insecure secrets.

content.html:

Setup essentials for local DApp development

Follow a practical path from scaffolding your frontend to connecting a local Hardhat node, installing Ethers.js, and keeping secrets out of your client bundle.

In this lesson

Scaffold a Next.js or React app, install Ethers.js, start Hardhat locally, and connect the frontend with a safe fallback provider.

Why it matters

A reproducible environment prevents lost time, secret leakage, and brittle deployments when smart contracts evolve across networks.

Who benefits

Frontend engineers, smart contract devs, and full-stack teams building DApps that need rapid local testing and clear deployment pipelines.

Outcome

A working Next.js or React DApp connected to a local Hardhat node and a set of best practices for secrets and contract addresses.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives outline the concrete skills you'll gain while setting up a DApp environment. First, you'll initialize a modern JavaScript project using tools such as create-react-app or create-next-app and understand when to choose React versus Next. js based on needs like server-side rendering. Second, you'll install and configure Web3 libraries, with an emphasis on Ethers. js for TypeScript-friendly APIs and smaller bundles, and you will see the basic install commands and reasoning. Third, you'll integrate a local blockchain environment such as Hardhat or Ganache so you can deploy and test contracts locally without gas fees. Fourth, you'll manage environment variables securely across development and production, using REACT_APP or NEXT_PUBLIC prefixes when client-side access is required. Each objective ties to a practical milestone: a scaffolded project, a working provider utility, a running local node, and a safe configuration strategy. These skills matter because they let you iterate faster, avoid leaking secrets, and maintain different configurations for staging and production. Keep these goals in mind as you follow the step-by-step examples and hands-on activity later in the chapter.

keyIdea.title: Practical milestones
keyIdea.text: By completing the objectives you produce a scaffolded DApp, a provider utility, a local node connection, and a secure environment configuration.

screens.title: Learning Objectives (Part 2)
screens.subtitle: Skills for maintainability, fallback providers, and secure deployments

narration.text: These next objectives focus on project hygiene and resilience. You will learn how to structure your project folders — components, hooks, utils, contracts and context — to keep Web3 logic separate from UI concerns. This structure makes it easier to update ABIs and redeploy contracts without breaking UI imports. You will implement a provider utility that first tries a browser wallet, then gracefully falls back to a read-only local JSON-RPC provider. That fallback improves user experience for people without MetaMask and supports automated tests. Finally, you'll apply secure environment variable patterns so A P I keys and private keys never accidentally become part of your client bundle. We will demonstrate the exact prefixes for both create-react-app and Next. js and show how to keep server-only secrets out of client code. These skills help you avoid common mistakes like exposing private keys or shipping the wrong contract address to production. Each objective includes a short verification step so you can check behavior locally before deploying.

keyIdea.title: Structure and resilience
keyIdea.text: Organize code and implement a wallet-first provider with a read-only fallback to create a robust development and test experience.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Learning Objectives

Maintainable structure

Separate components, hooks, utils, contracts, and context so updates to smart contracts do not ripple through unrelated UI code. This makes testing and CI integration simpler.

components/
hooks/
utils/
contracts/

Resilient provider

Build a utility that prefers a browser wallet for signing, and falls back to a JsonRpcProvider for read-only data when wallets are unavailable. This improves UX for non-wallet visitors.

Each objective above includes a verification step. For structure, create the folders and import an ABI from contracts/ into a test UI. For provider resilience, run the app without MetaMask and confirm you can still fetch contract state with a read-only provider.

screens.title: Initialize a React or Next.js DApp
screens.subtitle: Quick commands to scaffold a TypeScript frontend for your DApp

narration.text: Initializing a project is the first practical step. For simple single-page apps you can use create-react-app; for production-grade DApps that may need server-side rendering and routing, Next. js is preferred. Both tools scaffold a TypeScript-ready project with linting and build scripts. The key is choosing the right scaffold for your app's needs: use create-react-app for straightforward SPAs and fast prototyping, and choose Next. js when you want file-system routing, incremental static regeneration, or server-side code. A concrete example: run the create-next-app command with TypeScript and the App Router to get a production-friendly structure, then start the dev server. If you use create-react-app, you get a simple src/ and public/ layout that is easy to understand. After scaffolding, install Ethers. js and create a utils or context folder where Web3 connectivity will live. A common misconception is that Next. js is always more complicated; in practice, it pays off when you need SSR or edge-capable routes. Your verification step is to run the dev server, open the application in a browser, and confirm the development welcome page appears. That confirms the scaffold and build tooling are working before adding Web3 code.

keyIdea.title: Choose the right scaffold
keyIdea.text: Next.js for production features and SSR; create-react-app for quick prototypes. Start the dev server as a verification step.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Initialize a React or Next.js DApp
Commands
# Using create-react-app (for simpler SPAs)
npx create-react-app my-dapp-frontend --template typescript
cd my-dapp-frontend
npm start # or yarn start

# Using Next.js (recommended for production-grade DApps)
npx create-next-app@latest my-dapp-frontend --typescript --eslint --app
cd my-dapp-frontend
npm run dev # or yarn dev
Verification
  • Start the dev server and open the app at localhost:3000.
  • Confirm the welcome page renders before adding Web3 code.
Notes & Tips

Next.js provides file-system routing and server-side capabilities that are useful if your DApp needs pre-rendered pages or server-only secrets. create-react-app is simpler for single-page prototypes. After scaffolding, immediately create folders for components, hooks, utils, and contracts so your Web3 logic has a predictable place to live.

Key Takeaway

Scaffold with a purpose: pick the tool that matches your app's rendering and routing needs, then create a clean folder layout before adding blockchain code.

screens.title: Ethers.js versus Web3.js
screens.subtitle: Install commands and trade-offs for frontend Web3 libraries

narration.text: Choosing a Web3 library affects A P I ergonomics, bundle size, and TypeScript support. Ethers. js is preferred in modern DApp frontends because it has a cleaner A P I, better TypeScript types, and a smaller bundle footprint. Web3. js has served the ecosystem for longer and still works well, but it can be heavier and offers less ergonomic TypeScript support. Installation is straightforward: npm install ethers for Ethers. js or npm install web3 for Web3. js. After installing, organize your code by placing provider and signer logic into a utils or context file so UI components can import a ready-made connection. A common misunderstanding is that both libraries are interchangeable on every call; subtle A P I differences exist for handling providers, contract instances, and JSON-RPC formatting. Another practical note is bundle size: mobile users may benefit from Ethers. js's smaller footprint, and you can reduce impact further with lazy imports and code splitting. Finally, verify your install by importing a small A P I call in the browser console or a component to fetch a block number or network name. That quick check confirms the library is properly bundled and usable in the client.

keyIdea.title: Prefer Ethers.js for modern frontends
keyIdea.text: Ethers.js offers smaller bundles and TypeScript-friendly APIs; keep provider code centralized and verify with a simple RPC call.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Ethers.js vs Web3.js
Install
# Install Ethers.js
npm install ethers # or yarn add ethers

# Install Web3.js (alternative)
npm install web3 # or yarn add web3
Trade-offs
  • Ethers.js: cleaner API, TypeScript support, smaller bundle.
  • Web3.js: mature, widely used in older projects, larger bundle size.
Integration pattern

Place provider setup in src/utils or src/context and import it into pages or components. Prefer lazy loading wallet code to avoid large initial bundles.

Pro Tip

Test by calling provider.getBlockNumber() in a component or the console to confirm connectivity without building extra UI.

screens.title: Run a local Hardhat node
screens.subtitle: Start a local Ethereum network for fast testing and deployment

narration.text: A local node is the fastest way to iterate on smart contracts because you avoid real gas and network latency. Hardhat provides an integrated local network, testing framework, and deployment tooling. To start, create or open your Hardhat project and run npx hardhat node. That command launches a local JSON-RPC server typically at http://127.0.0.1:8545 and prints a set of funded test accounts. Your frontend can connect to this endpoint for read-only RPC calls, or connect via MetaMask if you point the wallet to the same local network. When you deploy contracts locally, note the deployed address and update your frontend's environment variable used during development. A common trap is assuming the local node persists deployments across restarts — by default, a fresh Hardhat node resets accounts and deployments, so record addresses or use scripts to redeploy as part of your dev workflow. Another issue is CORS: most Hardhat configurations allow connections from localhost, but if you use a different origin ensure your node accepts the request origin. Use the node output to copy an unlocked private key if you need a signer for programmatic transactions during testing, but never commit that private key into your repo.

keyIdea.title: Fast local development
keyIdea.text: Use npx hardhat node to run a local JSON-RPC server and test contracts quickly; track deployed addresses and avoid committing private keys.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Run a local Hardhat node
Start the node
# In your Hardhat project directory
npx hardhat node

# Typical RPC endpoint
http://127.0.0.1:8545
Hardhat prints funded accounts and private keys to the terminal. Use those private keys only for local testing and never commit them.
Usage patterns
  • Connect MetaMask to the local RPC for interactive testing and signing.
  • Use a JsonRpcProvider in the frontend for read-only access if no wallet is present.
  • Automate redeploys with scripts to avoid manual address tracking.
Common Mistake

Expecting deployments to persist across node restarts. Hardhat nodes reset state unless you snapshot or redeploy with scripts.

screens.title: Provider utility and wallet fallback
screens.subtitle: Accept a browser wallet or fallback to a local JsonRpcProvider

narration.text: Your frontend should choose the most appropriate provider at runtime. A typical pattern is to detect window. ethereum and prefer a browser wallet like MetaMask for signing transactions. If no wallet is available, fall back to a read-only JsonRpcProvider pointed at your local Hardhat node. Putting this logic into a single utility function simplifies your components and centralizes error handling. The provided code demonstrates how to import Ethers, test for window. ethereum, request account access, and return a provider and optional signer. One misconception is that a fallback provider can sign transactions; in most cases it cannot unless you configure a local Wallet with a private key. For local testing, you can attach a Wallet backed by a Hardhat account private key to the JsonRpcProvider when you require programmatic signing. Always avoid hardcoding private keys into source—use environment variables and keep server-only secrets off the client. To verify behavior, run the app with and without MetaMask and watch the console logs that indicate which provider was chosen. This guarantees reproducible, understandable provider selection across development setups. Provider utility and wallet fallback means detect window.ethereum for wallet signing; fallback to jsonrpcprovider for read-only operations, and only use local private keys for scripted tests.. In practical terms, accept a browser wallet or fallback to a local jsonrpcprovider. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Centralize provider logic
keyIdea.text: Detect window.ethereum for wallet signing; fallback to JsonRpcProvider for read-only operations, and only use local private keys for scripted tests.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Provider utility
Example utility (visual)
import { ethers } from "ethers";

let provider;
let signer;

export async function getWeb3Provider() {
  if (window.ethereum) {
    // User has MetaMask, connect to it
    provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
    signer = await provider.getSigner();
    console.log("Connected to MetaMask provider.");
  } else {
    // Fallback to a local Hardhat node for read-only operations
    provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider("http://127.0.0.1:8545");
    console.log("Connected to local Hardhat node (read-only).");
    // To send transactions programmatically, attach a Wallet with a local private key
    // const privateKey = "0xac0974..." // Example Hardhat private key
    // signer = new ethers.Wallet(privateKey, provider);
  }
  return { provider, signer };
}
Place this utility in src/utils/web3.js or src/app/utils/web3.ts and import it in components using an effect to initialize provider and optionally store the account.
Check
Run the app with MetaMask connected to your Hardhat node, then disconnect MetaMask and confirm the fallback message appears in console logs.
Key Takeaway

A single provider utility simplifies components and ensures a consistent fallback for read-only access when wallet injection is absent.

screens.title: Signers, private keys, and programmatic transactions
screens.subtitle: When to use a Wallet signer versus a browser wallet

narration.text: Understanding signers is central to performing transactions from your frontend or scripts. A browser wallet signer, provided by MetaMask through window. ethereum, requests explicit user approval for signatures and protects private keys from your application. This is the recommended flow for production user interactions. For automated tests and scripted deployments, you may attach a Wallet instance to a JsonRpcProvider using a private key, which lets your app programmatically sign transactions. However, never embed private keys in client-side code or commit them to source control. Instead, keep private keys and A P I secrets in server-side environment variables or a secure secret manager when possible. In local development, Hardhat prints test private keys you can use temporarily; prefer environment variables that are gitignored for any scripts. A common misconception is that programmatic signers are interchangeable with wallet signers; they differ by where the private key is kept and by user consent models. For verification, run a small script that deploys a contract using a Wallet signer and a separate UI that calls a read-only method with the JsonRpcProvider. That split demonstrates the different roles signers play during development and automated workflows.

keyIdea.title: Signer roles
keyIdea.text: Use browser wallets for user-driven signing and Wallet+provider for scripted deployments; never expose private keys in the client.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Signers & Private Keys
Architecture
Browser wallet signer
Runs in the user’s wallet, requests explicit user approvals, and never exposes private keys to the page.
Programmatic Wallet signer
Created with a private key and a JsonRpcProvider for scripts or automated deployments. Keep keys out of client bundles.
Use browser wallets for user-initiated txs and Wallet signers only for CI or local scripts. When using Wallet signers, read private keys from secure environment variables in server or CI environments.
Safety Note

Never commit private keys or include them in client-side code. Use .env and server-side secrets for automation.

Check

Run a deploy script with a Wallet signer and a separate UI read operation with JsonRpcProvider to observe both patterns working as intended.

screens.title: Manage environment variables securely
screens.subtitle: How React and Next.js handle client and server variables

narration.text: Environment variables let you separate configuration from code, which is critical for managing different contract addresses and A P I keys across development, staging, and production. For create-react-app, client variables must be prefixed with REACT_APP_ and are accessed via process. env. REACT_APP_CONTRACT_ADDRESS. For Next. js, use NEXT_PUBLIC_ for variables that must be available in the browser; variables without that prefix remain server-only. Put sensitive keys like Infura or Alchemy secrets in server-only variables and never expose private keys to client-side variables. During development, create a. env. local file and add it to. gitignore so secrets are not committed. A frequent mistake is assuming environment variables update at runtime in a deployed static site; you usually need to rebuild the app with the new environment values or use server runtime configuration for dynamic values. To validate setup, read the env value in your app and render the contract address in a non-sensitive debug area when running locally. This quick verification confirms the environment file is being loaded correctly and that you used the correct prefix for client accessibility. Manage environment variables securely means use react_app_ or next_public_ for client-side values and keep private keys in server-only variables to avoid accidental exposure.. In practical terms, how react and next.js handle client and server variables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Prefix matters
keyIdea.text: Use REACT_APP_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ for client-side values and keep private keys in server-only variables to avoid accidental exposure.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Manage environment variables
Create-React-App
# .env
REACT_APP_CONTRACT_ADDRESS=0xYourDeployedContractAddress
REACT_APP_INFURA_PROJECT_ID=your_infura_id

# Access: process.env.REACT_APP_CONTRACT_ADDRESS
Next.js
# .env.local
NEXT_PUBLIC_CONTRACT_ADDRESS=0xYourDeployedContractAddress
INFURA_PROJECT_ID=your_infura_id # server-side only

# Access: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_CONTRACT_ADDRESS
Common Mistake

Putting secrets in client-prefixed env vars exposes them to the browser. Use server-only variables for private keys and rotation-ready secrets.

screens.title: Organize your DApp for maintainability
screens.subtitle: A recommended folder layout for predictable development

narration.text: A disciplined project layout reduces friction when smart contracts evolve or when team members collaborate. A common and effective structure places UI elements in components/, hooks for reusable Web3 patterns in hooks/, utility functions such as provider setup in utils/, compiled ABIs or contract artifacts in contracts/, and global state or wallet context in context/. Keep pages or routes at the top level for Next. js. This separation prevents coupling between UI and contract details. For example, if you redeploy a contract and the address or ABI changes, only files in contracts/ and utils/ typically need updates; components import the updated utilities without modification. Add a scripts/ or deploy/ folder for Hardhat deployment scripts and a tests/ folder for contract tests. Avoid copying ABI JSON into many places — centralize ABI importing to one contracts/ location. For verification, change an ABI or address in contracts/ and rebuild; the UI should reflect the change without editing component code. This pattern helps automated CI pipelines, where deploy scripts emit addresses that can be consumed into environment variables or config files for the frontend.

keyIdea.title: Separation of concerns
keyIdea.text: Keep contracts, provider logic, hooks, and UI components in distinct folders so updates are localized and CI integration is easier.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Project Structure
Recommended layout
my-dapp-frontend/
├── public/
├── src/
│   ├── components/
│   ├── hooks/
│   ├── pages/ or app/
│   ├── utils/       # web3 provider, ABI loaders
│   ├── contracts/   # ABI artifacts copied from Hardhat
│   ├── context/     # wallet/provider context
│   └── styles/
├── scripts/         # deployment scripts
├── .env.local
└── package.json
Centralize contract artifacts and provider utilities so redeploys only require a small set of changes. Consider adding CI tasks to update frontend config after deployments.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Version mismatches, CORS, exposed keys, and ABI/address drift

narration.text: There are recurring pitfalls when setting up a DApp environment. Version mismatches between Node, npm/yarn, Hardhat, and Ethers. js can cause obscure runtime errors; check recommended versions in each tool's docs and pin versions in package. json or use an. nvmrc file. ABI and address drift happens when you redeploy contracts and forget to update the frontend; centralize ABI artifacts and update environment variables or a config file after each deployment. CORS issues are rare with local Hardhat nodes, but if you host the node separately ensure cross-origin requests are permitted for your frontend origin. Exposing private keys is a serious security error: never commit keys to git and never serve them from client-prefixed env variables. Another mistake is assuming window. ethereum will always exist; build a graceful fallback to a read-only provider so users without wallets can still view data. To avoid bundle bloat, consider lazy loading Web3 logic and only import heavy libraries when needed. Finally, write small verification tests: fetch a block number, read a known contract state, and confirm the behavior both with and without MetaMask connected. Those checks catch configuration issues early.

keyIdea.title: Prevent common errors
keyIdea.text: Pin versions, centralize ABIs/addresses, avoid exposing secrets, and implement a wallet fallback for better resilience.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Common mistakes
Checklist
  • Pin Node and package versions; use .nvmrc for Node.
  • Keep ABIs and addresses centralized and update after redeploys.
  • Never commit private keys; use server-side secrets.
  • Provide a read-only provider fallback when window.ethereum is absent.
Quick fixes
  • Resolve CORS by ensuring the node accepts your origin.
  • Reduce bundle size with lazy imports of Ethers.js where feasible.
  • Verify provider selection via console logs and a simple RPC call.
Key Takeaway

Many setup issues are avoided by simple verification steps: call an RPC method, read a contract value, and confirm provider selection with and without a wallet.

screens.title: Activity: Initialize Next.js and integrate Ethers.js
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step lab to connect a Next.js app to a local Hardhat node

narration.text: This activity walks you through a minimal, verifiable setup: scaffold a Next. js app, install Ethers. js, create a Hardhat project, deploy a simple contract, and connect the frontend with a utility file. Begin by running the create-next-app command with TypeScript and App Router. Install Ethers. js in the frontend. In a separate folder initialize Hardhat, create a simple contract with a greeting state, add a deploy script that prints the deployed address, and run npx hardhat node in one terminal. Deploy the contract to the local network and copy the address into your frontend’s. env. local using NEXT_PUBLIC_CONTRACT_ADDRESS. Then create src/app/utils/web3. ts that tries window. ethereum and falls back to http://127.0.0.1:8545. In the front page component import connectWeb3 in a useEffect hook and render the status and account if available. The verification steps are: start the Hardhat node, deploy, start Next. js dev server, and check the UI for connection messages. If MetaMask is connected, you should see the account; otherwise you should see a read-only connection to the local node. This activity is intentionally incremental so you can repeat it when contracts change.

keyIdea.title: Practice the full flow
keyIdea.text: Scaffold Next.js, install Ethers.js, start Hardhat, deploy, and connect the frontend to validate the end-to-end setup.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Hands-on Activity
Steps
  1. Scaffold Next.js with TypeScript: npx create-next-app@latest --typescript --app
  2. Install Ethers.js: npm install ethers
  3. Create Hardhat project, write contract, add deploy script
  4. Run npx hardhat node and deploy to localhost; copy address
  5. Add NEXT_PUBLIC_CONTRACT_ADDRESS in .env.local and start frontend
  6. Import connectWeb3 and confirm provider and account or fallback
Verification
  • Hardhat prints the deployed address in deploy script output.
  • The frontend console shows whether it connected to MetaMask or the local node.
  • The page displays a status string like Connected with account or Connected to local Hardhat node (read-only).
Try this

After setup, change the contract greeting, redeploy, and update NEXT_PUBLIC_CONTRACT_ADDRESS to validate how the frontend adapts to ABI/address changes.

screens.title: Deploy a contract with Hardhat
screens.subtitle: A small deployment script and how to use its output in the frontend

narration.text: Deploying locally is a repeatable step that ties your contract code to the frontend. Hardhat deploy scripts use the Ethers plugin to get a contract factory, deploy it, and print the address. The example deploy. js creates a MyContract factory, deploys the contract, awaits deployment, and prints the deployed address. After deployment, copy the address into your frontend’s environment variable used for development. One subtle point is that the ABI must also be accessible to the frontend; copy the ABI file from Hardhat’s artifacts into your frontend contracts/ folder or export a minimal JSON contract artifact as part of your build pipeline. A common misconception is that the deployment address is stable; in local networks it changes every deploy so automating the transfer of addresses to the frontend is helpful for continuous testing. To verify a deployment, call a read-only contract method from the frontend using your provider and confirm expected state. This process stitches together the contract artifacts, the deployed address, and the frontend provider so the UI can interact with the contract instance. Deploy a contract with Hardhat means deploy with hardhat scripts, copy the address and abi to the frontend, and verify by calling a read-only method.. In practical terms, a small deployment script and how to use its output in the frontend. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Connect deployment to the UI
keyIdea.text: Deploy with Hardhat scripts, copy the address and ABI to the frontend, and verify by calling a read-only method.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Deploy Script
Example deploy.js
const hre = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const MyContract = await hre.ethers.getContractFactory("MyContract");
  const myContract = await MyContract.deploy();
  await myContract.waitForDeployment();

  console.log(`MyContract deployed to: ${myContract.target}`);
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
After running the script with --network localhost, copy the printed address into your .env.local as NEXT_PUBLIC_CONTRACT_ADDRESS and ensure the frontend imports the contract ABI from contracts/.
Verification
Call a read-only method like greeting in the deployed MyContract from the frontend and confirm the returned value matches the contract state.
Pro Tip

Automate address propagation to the frontend with a small script that writes .env.local after deployment during local CI or dev workflows.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Keep five core ideas in mind as you set up your DApp environment. First, choose the right frontend scaffold—Next. js for production features and create-react-app for simple prototypes. Second, prefer Ethers. js for smaller bundles and TypeScript support, but know Web3. js remains an option. Third, run a local Hardhat node for fast, cost-free testing, and remember deployments on local nodes are ephemeral unless preserved. Fourth, centralize provider and signer logic so components remain simple and a graceful fallback to a JsonRpcProvider exists when window. ethereum is absent. Fifth, manage environment variables carefully: use REACT_APP_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ for client-accessible values and keep private keys and server-only secrets out of the client bundle. These ideas reduce friction, improve security, and make your DApp easier to maintain and test. When you next scaffold a project, apply each concept step by step and verify connections with simple RPC calls and deploy scripts.

keyIdea.title: Five foundations
keyIdea.text: Project scaffold, Web3 library, local node, centralized provider logic, and secure env management are the pillars of a strong DApp environment.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Key Concepts
Frontend Frameworks
React/Next.js provide structure; pick Next.js when you need SSR or advanced routing.
Ethers.js / Web3.js
Ethers.js is lighter and TypeScript-friendly; install and centralize provider code in utils/.
Local Blockchain
Use Hardhat or Ganache to deploy and test contracts locally without real costs.
Final takeaway
Structure projects for maintenance, centralize provider and contract artifacts, and protect secrets with proper environment management.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three quick reminders before you code

narration.text: Before you start coding, keep three concise reminders: always centralize and version contract artifacts and addresses so redeploys are easy to manage; implement a provider utility that prefers a browser wallet but gracefully falls back to a read-only JsonRpcProvider so users without wallets can still view data; and never expose private keys or server-only A P I keys in client-prefixed environment variables. These practices make your development iterations faster, your deployments safer, and your team collaboration less error-prone. When you finish the hands-on activity, run simple verification steps: confirm the Hardhat node prints funded accounts, confirm the frontend console logs the provider selection, and confirm a read-only contract call returns expected state. Those checks give immediate confidence that your environment is correctly wired. What to Remember means centralize artifacts, implement a wallet-first fallback provider, and never expose private keys in client bundles.. In practical terms, three quick reminders before you code. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Centralize artifacts, implement a wallet-first fallback provider, and never expose private keys in client bundles.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What to Remember
Centralize artifacts
Keep ABIs and addresses in contracts/ and update them on redeploys.
Wallet-first fallback
Detect window.ethereum and fallback to JsonRpcProvider for read-only access if needed.
Protect secrets
Store private keys server-side and use environment variables with correct prefixes for client values.
Quick verification
Check the Hardhat node output, validate provider selection in the console, and fetch a contract value from the UI.
